judge_assessment.explanation: Both hard failures are exact, and the first understates the gap. Problem 2 asks for each zero, its MULTIPLICITY, and whether the graph crosses or touches at each; verify.json id 2 is a bare zeros list, expected [-1, 3]. As the judge says, a zero list cannot distinguish multiplicity 2 from multiplicity 1 — (x+1)(x-3)^2 and (x+1)(x-3) produce the identical list. Problem 5 is worse than the judge reports: it asks for the DEGREE of p, each zero with its multiplicity, and whether the graph crosses, touches or flattens, and id 5 is again a bare zeros list [0, 4] — so the degree (5), both multiplicities (2 and 3) and all three behaviour labels are unverified, four printed answers behind one check. The second failure is exact: problems 4 and 8 each end with an explicit 'say in one sentence' demand and each id carries only its two limit entries, while id 10 is the sole manual entry in the file. I recomputed everything in SymPy — the two factorisations, all four limits, both constructed polynomials, the quartic's four roots, and the root multiplicities of x^2(x-4)^3 and x(x+2)^2(x-3) — and all agree with the key. REJECT is correct.

strengths_to_preserve: The header figure is the right figure and it renders cleanly at 80 dpi: three unlabelled local shapes — a line crossing, a parabola touching, a cubic flattening through — with no values on them and a caption that says so ('No values shown: use the factors given in each problem'). It teaches the shape vocabulary without doing any problem's work for it.

Problem 5 is deliberately the one that needs all three labels at once: x^2(x-4)^3 has an even multiplicity and an odd multiplicity greater than one in the same polynomial, so 'touch' and 'flatten as it passes' cannot be conflated.

Problems 6 and 9 invert the task — given the crossing/bouncing behaviour, construct the least-degree monic polynomial — which is the strongest available test that multiplicity has been understood rather than recited.
Problem 8's 'say why both ends behave the same way here but not in problem 4' explicitly links two items, which is what makes end behaviour a rule rather than two memorised answers.

id 10's manual entry is a model of how these should read: it names exactly what the reviewer must see — 'touches the axis at x = -2, crosses at x = 0 and at x = 3, and rises on both ends (degree 4, positive leading coefficient)' — rather than just saying 'graph, check by eye'.

root_causes.description: The `zeros` type returns a SET of roots, which is structurally incapable of expressing the thing this worksheet is about. Multiplicity is discarded by the type itself, so on a multiplicity sheet the check that satisfies the coverage gate is the one check guaranteed to miss the topic. Nothing in the contract notices that the declared facet is 'multiplicity-behavior' while the entry type cannot represent multiplicity.
evidence: SKILL.md:189 — 'verification hard-fails unless every problem id 1..N has at least one check (use `manual` for the unverifiable ones), so a partially-verified answer key can never slip through'. The trailing promise does not follow from the rule: the rule counts PROBLEMS, the promise is about ANSWERS.
scripts/verify.py:2020 — the coverage gate is `missing = [i for i in range(1, problem_count + 1) if i not in ids]`, i.e. membership of the id set, never a count of printed response slots

tests/check_layout.py:47-49 and ANSWER_RE at :99 — the layout gate requires that each item CONTAIN one answer-location macro; it never compares that count against the number of verify entries carrying the id
verify.json id 2: {"type": "zeros", "expr": "(x+1)*(x-3)**2", "expected": [-1, 3]} — the exponent 2 is present in the expression and absent from the expected value
verify.json id 5: {"type": "zeros", "expr": "x**2*(x-4)**3", "expected": [0, 4]} against a stem demanding degree, two multiplicities and three behaviour labels
verify.json ids 2, 5 and 10 all carry "facet": "multiplicity-behavior" while using a type that erases multiplicity

root_causes.description: SKILL.md's rationing language for `manual` is what leaves problems 4 and 8 undeclared, and the sheet proves the author knew better — id 10 carries a careful manual entry, so the pattern was available and simply not applied to the one-sentence demands.
evidence: SKILL.md:249 — 'Reserve `manual` for genuinely open reasoning (proofs, "explain why", construction)'. 'Reserve' is rationing language and is what an author follows when deciding a single sentence is not worth a manual entry.

SKILL.md:257 — 'Use `manual` for: graph sketches, sign charts, word problem setups, two-column proofs, constructions, Riemann sum tables, series convergence arguments, and any explanation/reasoning answer.' This clause is broad and correct, and it is the one that is being ignored.
Neither line is enforced: no gate reads the worksheet prose for an imperative like 'explain', 'say in one sentence', 'name the error' or 'state whether'

worksheet.tex problem 4 'say in one sentence which two features of the polynomial decided them' and problem 8 'say in one sentence why both ends behave the same way here but not in problem 4' — neither id carries a manual entry

answer_key.pdf problem 4 prints 'Expected sentence: “The odd degree makes the ends opposite; the negative leading coefficient decides which end goes down.”' — the author wrote the reviewer's model answer and still declared no manual entry

improvements.title: Every printed response slot needs its own verification entry, not one per problem
improvements.proposed_change: Give multiplicity a representable form and require it when the facet claims it. Two parts: (a) extend the `zeros` type to accept a mapping as well as a list — {"expected": {"-1": 1, "3": 2}} — validated against sympy.roots(), which already returns exactly that dict (I confirmed roots((x+1)*(x-3)**2) == {-1: 1, 3: 2}); (b) in verify.py's facet consistency gate, reject a problem tagged facet 'multiplicity-behavior' whose only entries are list-form `zeros`. Problem 5's degree also needs its own entry, which the existing schema already supports as an eval. This is additive: the list form stays legal for problems that genuinely only ask for the zero set. Fold in the same sheet's smaller instance of this key while the file is open: problems 1 and 3 say 'Factor ... completely, then list every real zero', and ids 1 and 3 are `factor` entries only, so the zero lists (0, 2, -2 and 0, 5, -2) are printed answers with nothing behind them — an internal inconsistency, since problem 7 makes the same demand and IS verified as a `solve`. Each needs a companion `zeros` entry.
improvements.regression_test: Add a verify.py unit test asserting that {"type": "zeros", "expr": "(x+1)*(x-3)**2", "expected": [-1, 3]} FAILS when the entry is tagged facet 'multiplicity-behavior', and that the dict form {"-1": 1, "3": 2} passes. Today the list form passes unconditionally.
improvements.expected_impact: Restores verification of the sheet's actual subject on ids 2, 5 and 10. It is the difference between checking that the student found the right x-values and checking that they read the exponent, which is the whole standard (HSA-APR.B.3).
improvements.risk: Medium. Changing an existing type's accepted shape risks breaking sheets across the corpus, so the dict form must be purely additive and the facet-based requirement must land warn-only for one run. sympy.roots() can return an incomplete dict for high-degree or irrational cases; fall back to MANUAL rather than FAIL when its multiplicities do not sum to the degree.

improvements.title: Written explanations the worksheet demands are recorded as machine-verified rather than manual
improvements.proposed_change: Declare ids 4 and 8 manual alongside their limit entries. Both stems end in an explicit 'say in one sentence' and both already have a model answer written in the key ('Expected sentence: ...'), so the reviewer criterion is a copy. Enforce it generally with the prose scan under this key, and merge SKILL.md:249 into :257 so 'any explanation/reasoning answer' is the single rule.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem whose stem ends 'say in one sentence which two features decided them' with only limit entries for its id; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero. Silent today.
improvements.expected_impact: Moves the sheet from 1 manual item to 3, which is the honest count, and makes the key's already-written 'Expected sentence' lines reachable as reviewer criteria rather than decoration.
improvements.risk: Medium; keyword scans over-fire on directions text. Scope to \problem segments, ship warn-only first.

improvements.title: Integer answers print with an ASCII hyphen while the neighbouring symbolic answers use a real minus sign
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, `_fmt()` returns bare `str(v)` for the int/Decimal branch and `repr(v)` for floats, so a negative number reaches LaTeX as text-mode '-3'. Every string expected, by contrast, goes through `sympy.latex(sympy.sympify(v))` and gets a proper math-mode minus. Wrap the numeric branches in math mode the same way — return '$' + str(v) + '$' (Decimal formatting is preserved because the string is built before the wrap, so a verified 6.30 still prints 6.30). Do it for int, Decimal and float alike.
improvements.regression_test: Add a case to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py rendering a verify JSON with {"id": 1, "expected": -3} and {"id": 2, "expected": "x - 7"}, and assert both rendered entries contain the same minus token (i.e. entry 1 is '$-3$', not the bare '-3'). It fails today: entry 1 renders '-3' in text mode and entry 2 renders '$x - 7$'.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes a visible inconsistency inside a single bank. In this slice alone it shows in curr-352 ('5. -1' beside '8. 7 - 24i'), curr-363, curr-369, curr-382, curr-388 and curr-400.
improvements.risk: Low. The bank is plain text by design and is never read by check_answer_key.py, so the strict per-problem answer-key binding cannot be affected. The only failure mode is a LaTeX compile error, which the existing compile-ak gate catches on the same run.

case_summary: The polynomial mathematics is correct — factorisations, all four end-behaviour limits, both constructed polynomials, the biquadratic's four roots and every multiplicity recomputed and matching. The teaching design is strong: an unlabelled three-shape reference figure, a problem (5) that forces 'touch' and 'flatten' apart within one polynomial, and two inverse construction problems. The rejection is well founded and the first hard failure understates it: the `zeros` type discards multiplicity by construction, so on a sheet whose declared facet is 'multiplicity-behavior' the entries that satisfy the coverage gate are precisely the ones that cannot express the topic. Problem 5 hides four printed answers (degree, two multiplicities, three behaviour labels) behind one two-element list. Problems 4 and 8 demand explanations with no manual entry, though the key writes out the model sentence for problem 4. Beyond the judge, problems 1 and 3 ask for zero lists that go unverified while the parallel problem 7 is verified.
